messages.body_plain:
Hi Karen,

On 6/7/2014 7:55 AM, Karen Ertrachter wrote:
> Hi everyone,
> I'm working on a model and I'm not able to assess model fit since it 
> will not produce MCMC diagnostics.  Instead, I typically get the error 
> message that 'MCMC diagnostics were not used or stored' and gof 
> doesn't work properly either. The gof code will run, but it just runs 
> for a while without showing anything or manages to shut down R.  In 
> the past, I was able to get MCMC diagnostics, so I'm wondering how to 
> fix this.
The model you are fitting is a purely dyadic independent one, since it 
only contains edges, nodematch and nodefactor terms.  That is, it posits 
that the only influence on a tie's probability are the nodes of the two 
adjacent actors; as such the ties are all conditionally independent. 
Because of this, logistic regression works perfectly. The ergm algorithm 
detects this automatically, and doesn't need to run the MCMC to obtain 
the fit. As a result, there are no diagnostics. You don't really need to 
diagnostics for such a model, because it is guaranteed to fit; there are 
no potential issues with degeneracy or other forms of lack of 
convergence.  If you'd like to fit the MCMC anyway and obtain 
diagnostics on it, you can by adding:

force.main=T

inside your control.ergm argument.

As for the gof issues, that's harder to diagnose.  It may simply be that 
your network is very large, and taking 100 simulations of it (the 
default) and then calculating the distance matrix on it takes a long 
long time and/or more memory than you have. I would fist try this:

gofjmodel1 <- gof(jmodel.1, control=control.gof.ergm(nsim=10), verbose=T)

That will reduce the number of simulations in the gof down to 10, and 
also give you feedback in between each one.

If you are still having troubles, you might try removing the distance 
component of the gof to see if you can at least get the others easily.  
That is, pass the gof elements you *do* want to include with a formula, 
as such:

gofjmodel1 <- gof(jmodel.1~ degree+espartners.....)

where the ones you pick will depend on whether your network is directed 
or not (and are listed at ?gof).  Note that if you do this, you also 
need to change the control argument from control.gof.ergm to 
control.gof.formula.  Yes, we know that part is a bit counter-intuitive, 
but it fits in with standard R practice.

HTH,
Steve

kludgey, but I think this gets you what you want -- no need to use sna:

aaa <- matrix(floor(5*runif(25)), 5,5) 		# random integer matrix

m <- max(aaa) 					# the max

aaa[lower.tri(aaa)] <- t(aaa[upper.tri(aaa)]) 	# symmetrize binary matrix
aaa <- m*aaa 					# multiply by max

Hi James, Thomas, and others who are interested.

First, thanks for you help. I guess my case was a little different than how
you guys did it, so I built off of your advice and came up with the
following.

#This code symmetrizes a valued matrix by max or min values of ij-ji. For
max, steps 1 & 5 should use "-999" & step 3 must use ">" and ">=". For min,
use "999", "<", & "<=" respectively. The input data must use NA rather than
0 for non-ties. The code uses weak symmetrization, so an NA in ij or ji
will be replaced with valued data of ji or ij respectively.

#make a sample matrix that includes NAs and set diag to 0.
test<-matrix(ncol=10, nrow=10, sample(c(NA, 1:5), 100, replace=TRUE,
c(.5,rep(.1,5)))) #NA has high prob
#test<-matrix(ncol=10, nrow=10, 5, 100) #to test with full mat of single
values if desired
test0<-diag.remove(test, remove.val=0) ;test0

#Step 1: convert NA to "999" for use with "<" and "-999" for use with ">"
so NA gets replaced with desired tie value (i.e., weak symmetrization)
test0[is.na(test0)]<- (-999) ;test0

#Step 2: separate lower and upper tri
low<-upper.tri.remove(test0, remove.val=NA) ;low
upp<-lower.tri.remove(test0, remove.val=NA) ;upp

#Step 3: get min (<) or max (>) based on True/False, convert to 1/0, and
combine lower and upper. To deal with ij=ji, upp2 uses <= or >=, step2 uses
NA, and NAs are converted to 0 in step3. This avoids "full = 1+1"
low2 <- (ifelse((low > t(upp))==TRUE, 1, 0));low2[is.na(low2)]<- 0 ;low2
upp2 <- (ifelse((upp >= t(low))==TRUE, 1, 0));upp2[is.na(upp2)]<- 0 ;upp2
full <- (upp2 + low2) ;full

#Step 4: extract from original data using full binary mat (selects min/max
based on above choice (< or >))
tempNet <- test0*full ;tempNet

#Step 5: final symmetrized mat based on min or max as specified above.
Then, just in case there were any NA-NA ij-ji pairs, convert those to 0
final <- tempNet + t(tempNet)
final[final == -999] <- 0 ;final

Hi statnet users,

I write with another question. I am having trouble working with valued data
for network objects. Example code below. Basically, I have a full matrix
with tie values and I am using NAs for non-ties. This is a non-symmetric
network.

I want to convert the matrix to a network object, remove isolates, and then
convert back to a matrix. The problem is that when I convert the network
object back to a matrix I get all binary values. The valued data is lost.

Here is example code. Note, the code below just uses a random matrix for
sample data, so there may be no isolates to remove. But this does not
matter as you will still see that the valued ties become 1s after they are
passed through the network object.

#make a sample matrix that includes NAs and set diag to 0.
test<-matrix(ncol=10, nrow=10, sample(c(NA, 1:5), 100, replace=TRUE,
c(.5,rep(.1,5)))) #NA has high prob
test0<-diag.remove(test, remove.val=0) ;test0

#make as network object and try to keep valued data using ignore.eval
testMeNet<-as.network.matrix(test0, ignore.eval=FALSE, na.rm=TRUE)
;testMeNet

#find isolates
isos <- isolates(testMeNet, diag=FALSE)
length(isos)

#remove isolates
testMeCut<-delete.vertices(testMeNet, (isolates(testMeNet, diag=FALSE)))
;testMeCut

#convert back to matrix. Problem is, valued ties are lost. They are now 1s
testMeOut <- as.matrix(testMeCut) ;testMeOut

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dominic - if you have a binary variable, and an edges term and a 
nodefactor term for that variable, then you only have one degree of 
freedom left.  That means that you can only do nodematch with diff=F, 
not with diff=T.  Note how in that paper we do diff=T for Grade and Race 
because there are multiple categories, but not for Sex, because there 
aren't enough degrees of freedom.

The reason why there are only three degrees of freedom is that there are 
only three kinds of partnerships with regard to combinations on a binary 
attribute: 00, 01, and 11.

Hope that helps,
Steve

There are two ways to address your error:

1. Implement structural zeros using the extreme value detection.

detect it and fix the coefficient to -Inf.  You will get a warning

Model_02 <- ergm(Y ~ edges + b1star(2) + edgecov(Z))

be a bug in the last step of the estimate causing your error.
Model_03 <- ergm(Y ~ edges + b1star(2) + offset(edgecov(Z)) ,
offset.coef=-Inf, eval.loglik=FALSE )
